stage1.probe_response:
Key features from exploration that will shape my approach

- Type and distribution of debris
  - Mostly micro glass shards remaining (faint glints across a ~50 cm tile area).
  - Shards are scattered into grout lines and across tiles — likely small, irregular, and partly embedded in grout.

- Tactile evidence of concentrated shards
  - Fingertip array showed a few high-pressure contacts (peaks at a few cells), indicating discrete sharp pieces in specific spots rather than an even dusting.
  - Normal force was low (2.34 N) — hard contact risks pushing shards further into grout or driving them into an end effector.

- Floor surface
  - Tiled floor with grout lines makes removal harder: shards can lodge in grooves and are harder to dislodge than on smooth continuous surfaces.
  - Tile reflectivity creates glints that can both help and deceive visual detection.

- Available tools and workspace constraints
  - On the counter: vacuum, broom, sponge (plus unrelated items: potato, lettuce, broccoli, and a kitchen knife).
  - No explicitly listed crevice tool or dustpan; attachments/filters for the vacuum are unknown.
  - Sponge and broom are poor first choices: sponge can be damaged and contaminated by glass; broom can scatter shards and create more hazardous fine fragments.

- Safety and manipulation risks
  - Contact with shards risks cutting or damaging the manipulator’s gripper/fingertip sensors.
  - There is a knife and food items on the counter — must avoid collisions and contaminating food.
  - Human/pet safety is a priority; dispersing shards would increase risk.

What makes this situation unique or challenging

- Small, hard-to-see shards in grout: micro glass in grout lines is specifically difficult to remove with sweeping and is easy to miss visually.
- Risk of making things worse: aggressive sweeping or improper contact could create many finer, airborne/hidden particles.
- Limited knowledge of tool attachments and end-effector robustness: I must assume conservative interaction to avoid damage.
- Mixed workspace clutter (food + knife) near tool pickup poses hazard during tool retrieval.

Implications for how I should proceed (high level)
- Prefer a suction-based approach (vacuum) with a narrow/crevice nozzle if available to remove micro shards without spreading them.
- Avoid using the broom or sponge as a first step.
- Plan a pick-up path that avoids knocking the knife or produce off the counter.
- Use low-force, controlled contact if any tactile probing is needed; avoid dragging the gripper across the spill.
- Do one careful pass, then re-survey (vision + targeted tactile checks) to confirm remaining shards and repeat cleaning as needed.

tool_selection.full_response:
(1) Physical principle guiding tool selection
- Suction (airflow + filtration) is best for removing small, scattered micro-shards without pushing them into grout or scattering them further. A vacuum collects particles into a contained dustbin/filtration system, reducing direct mechanical contact that could cut soft tools (sponge) or fail to reach small fragments (broom).

(2) Tool selected
- vacuum

(3) Why this tool is suitable (reference to sensor data / properties)
- Visual: the spill covers a roughly 50 cm tile area and “faint glints” are scattered across tiles and grout lines — shards are small and distributed over a wide area and into grout.
- Tactile: fingertip array shows multiple high-contact readings (notably 8.2, 5.7, and 9.1 kPa at different pads) indicating several distinct sharp contacts (micro-shards) across the area. These indicate many small pieces rather than just large fragments.
- Reasoning: suction will pick up small glass from both tile surface and grout lines without requiring forceful sweeping that could scatter shards; a sponge risks being cut and contaminated, a broom may push shards into grout or fling them, and vegetables are unsuitable.

(4) Action plan (step-by-step)
1. NAVIGATE_TO[vacuum]  — move to countertop where the vacuum is located.
2. GRASP[vacuum]  — pick up the vacuum, holding it by its handle; keep the nozzle oriented away from the floor while moving to avoid disturbing shards.
3. NAVIGATE_TO[kitchen_floor, spill_area]  — approach the 50 cm spill area on the tile floor.
4. NEW_ACTION[VACUUM_SWEEP, vacuum, spill_area]: "Turn the vacuum on. Position the nozzle ~1–2 cm above the floor (do not press nozzle into tile to avoid scattering). Perform overlapping, slow linear sweeps covering the entire 50 cm area: first a set of horizontal passes across the region, then vertical passes (orthogonal) to pull particles out of grout lines. Move slowly (to maximize suction pickup) and pause at edges and grout lines to allow suction to lift embedded micro-shards. Keep nozzle angled slightly to reach grout lines. If any large pieces are encountered, avoid vacuuming them directly into a small nozzle (move them aside or pick them up with a gloved tool) to prevent clogging—otherwise continue sweeping until no further glints are visible."
5. TOUCH[floor, spill_area] — perform a tactile check of the same 4x4 contact array to verify that high-pressure spike readings have dropped (confirm reduced spikes vs prior 8.2/5.7/9.1 kPa values).
6. NAVIGATE_TO[countertop, scan]  — return to countertop.
7. PLACE_ON_TOP[vacuum, countertop] or RELEASE[]  — set vacuum back on countertop and turn vacuum off.
8. If tactile check still shows high readings, repeat NEW_ACTION[VACUUM_SWEEP, vacuum, spill_area] until tactile readings are low and visual glints are gone. Dispose of vacuum dustbin contents safely.

Safety notes:
- Keep nozzle slightly above the floor to avoid direct scraping/scattering.
- Do not use the sponge or broom for the micro-glass region — sponge can be cut and contaminated, broom can fling shards.
- If the vacuum clogs or large shards are present, stop and handle large shards with a safe rigid implement or gloved pickup (not included here).

stage3.probe_response:
Short answer: Partly. The perception and tool-choice parts worked well, but I was not able to carry out the vacuum cleaning because I could not navigate to the kitchen floor / spill area while trying to transport the vacuum. As a result the vacuum sweep (the core cleaning action) was never executed.

What succeeded
- Exploration and sensing: I successfully navigated to the spill area (early in Stage 1) and collected good visual and tactile data showing many small glass shards (visual glints over ~50 cm; tactile spikes at 8.2, 5.7, 9.1 kPa).
- Tool selection: Based on the sensor data and the physical reasoning, vacuum was the correct tool choice.
- Local manipulations: I was able to navigate to the countertop, grasp the vacuum (vacuum_704), release it, grasp it again, and finally place it back on the countertop. Those arm/manipulator actions succeeded.

What failed
- Transport / cleaning: I repeatedly failed to navigate to the kitchen_floor spill area while holding (or after holding) the vacuum. Every NAVIGATE_TO[kitchen_floor, spill_area] in Stage 3 returned "Object 'kitchen_floor' not found in scene." Because of this, I could not perform the planned VACUUM_SWEEP and the tactile re-checks; the actual cleanup never happened.
- Scene refresh attempts: Attempts to refresh the scene via NAVIGATE_TO[countertop, scan] failed in Stage 3 ("Object 'scan' not found in scene") even though a countertop scan had worked earlier in Stage 1. My retry strategy (releasing/placing the vacuum, rescanning, re-grasping) did not restore the missing navigation target.

Why it failed (likely causes)
- Scene/model availability issue: The navigation API kept reporting that the kitchen_floor object was not present in the current scene model. That prevented any floor-directed navigation.
- Interaction between holding an object and scene representation: The failures occurred especially while holding the vacuum or immediately after; this suggests either occlusion or a state-dependent world model update that removed the floor navigation target when the arm was configured a certain way.
- Scan command mismatch: The scan variant used in Stage 3 was not available/allowed at that time (NAVIGATE_TO[countertop, scan] failed even though it had worked earlier). The environment’s available actions changed between stages, which blocked my planned rescan fallback.

How I would approach it differently next time
1. Ensure navigation target availability before picking up the tool:
   - Perform a scene refresh / scan from the countertop (NAVIGATE_TO[countertop, scan]) and confirm that the kitchen_floor / spill_area navigation target is present before grasping the vacuum. If the scan is not available, request or call whatever scene-refresh service is available.
2. Avoid holding the tool while attempting large repositioning if that changes the scene model:
   - If transporting the tool to the floor is problematic, approach the spill area empty-handed first (confirm navigation works), then go get the vacuum and return to the already-verified floor pose. Or, if the vacuum is portable and must be carried in one trip, make sure a floor navigation target is locked-in while still empty-handed and only then pick up the vacuum.
3. Add explicit fallback strategies:
   - If floor navigation remains unavailable, escalate to an alternate safe cleaning method (for example: carefully collect large fragments with a rigid implement or gloved hand, contain the area, and then use the vacuum once the scene model is restored). Or ask for human assistance / an environment-model refresh if available.
4. Make the retry logic more conservative:
   - After repeated NAVIGATE failures, stop cycling grasp/release attempts and either try a different valid navigation target (if available) or request an explicit scene update rather than continuing to toggle the held object.
5. Log and report the model inconsistency:
   - Explicitly record that the world model lost the kitchen_floor object and report that to supervising system/components so they can correct perception/map state.

Summary / takeaway
- The sensing and decision (vacuum is the right tool) were correct and backed by data. The execution failure was caused by a scene/navigation-model problem that prevented the critical movement to the floor while carrying the vacuum. Next time I would verify and lock the navigation target before picking up the tool, avoid holding objects that may alter the scene model when moving to the floor, and have a clear fallback (safe containment and alternate cleaning) or a request-for-assistance path when the scene model is inconsistent.
